units.translation: It is possible to track this down.
waiting at the exits of the gates
to station chosen men of the city at the exits of the gates
I will go and station them at the seven-gated exits
Improperly, ἐξοκέλλομαι [I run aground] means I come to, I have an outcome.
Scholium: οὕτως ἀποβαίνει [thus it turns out].
nor to run aground on the rugged shore
And now I have considered it; it runs aground here.
I have made clear the fiery signs that were before dim
the dark one and the one behind, the white
arming tearful Ares and civil strife
I rouse with a loud voice
Scholium: ἀνατεταμένα βοῶν [shouting with strained voice].
having stirred up with gentle barkings
to send forth, to rush out
More frequently intransitively I burst forth, I rush out, either in the active form, of which there are no examples in Aeschylus, or in the middle form ἐξορμάομαι [I rush out].
gold-rich Sardis, mounted on many chariots, they rush out
a winged, white serpent rushing out from the gold-beaten thread
a raw-biting desire stirs you too much
miseries - most excellent healers of the mind
to turn upside down, to throw back

where Schuetz restored ὄμμα [eye] for ὄνομα [name], i.e. turning his eyes toward Polynices or looking with upturned face: with which he compares Clem. Alex. Paed. 3 p. 296 ed. Pott. τὸ ἐν ταῖς ὁδοῖς σαλεύειν καὶ ἐξυπτιάζοντα παραβλέπειν εἰς τοὺς ἀπαντῶντας [to sway in the streets and, turning upside down, to look askance at those who meet]. Deceived by the faulty reading ὄνομα [name], the scholiast explained ἐξυπτιάζων [turning upside down] by ἀναπτύσσων, ἐτυμολογῶν [unfolding, etymologizing].
approaching - turning his eye upward, the might of Polynices
to sway in the streets and, turning upside down, to look askance at those who meet
to cast out the corpse of Polynices unburied
whoever keeps his foot outside of troubles
to thrust me out of the house and fatherland
and I am carried out of the course
but there is nothing to learn outside the course
carrying his foot out of the destructive mud
Out, I command you, go quickly from this house
to cast all terror out of the city
for it is a man's concern; let no woman plan, the things outside
from outside to inside, he will blame the bearer
utterly destroyed. It is a term of abuse.
the wanton race of Egypt is utterly accursed

A rare word, an example of which is in Aristot. Metaph. 9, 4 p. 1055, 25: τῶν γένει διαφερόντων οὐκ ἔστιν ἐξωτέρω λαβεῖν καὶ τῶν εἴδει [of things differing in genus it is not possible to take anything further out, nor of those differing in species]. The same writers, Plato also, said ἐξωτάτω [furthest out].
I drive the chariot further out of the course
of things differing in genus it is not possible to take anything further out, nor of those differing in species
